name: Catalan
summary:
Catalan is a Western Romance language indigenous to the eastern Iberian Peninsula and Western Mediterranean islands. It is the official and co-official language of Catalonia, the Balearic Islands, and the Valencian Community in Spain, the sole official language of Andorra, and a recognized language in the Sardinian city of Alghero (Italy). With approximately 10 million native speakers and 4 million additional speakers, Catalan is one of Europe's largest minority languages.

Catalan descended from Vulgar Latin and began diverging from its Gallo-Romance cousins (French, Occitan) in the 8th–10th centuries CE. Medieval Catalan literature flourished under the Crown of Aragon, producing the 13th-century philosopher Ramon Llull — the first major author to write philosophy in a European vernacular — and a rich tradition of troubadour poetry, chronicles, and spiritual literature. The union of the Crowns of Aragon and Castile (1479) began Catalan's political subordination, but it remained a vigorous literary and legal language.

Catalan identity became politically charged from the 18th century onward. The New Plant decrees of Philip V (1716) suppressed Catalan in official life after Catalonia backed the losing side in the War of Spanish Succession. The 19th-century Renaixença (Renaissance) revived Catalan literary culture; Franco's dictatorship (1939–1975) banned public use of Catalan. The post-Franco Statute of Autonomy (1979) restored Catalan as co-official language. The independence movement (2010s), culminating in the unilateral declaration of independence (2017) that Spain declared void, has made Catalan the most politically charged language in contemporary Europe.
